::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Early-life adversity, childhood loneliness, and educational achievement: A prospective study
table.research_questions: We hypothesize that children reporting persistent loneliness will more often come from poorer socioenvironmental contexts (i.e., higher material hardship, poorer neighborhood conditions, and more frequent emotional and physical child maltreatment), and will have lower verbal ability compared to those who never reported loneliness or did it at only one measurement point (transient loneliness). Moreover, we expect that children who report persistent loneliness during childhood will be at a higher risk of poorer educational achievement compared to the never-lonely and transient-lonely groups, even after considering initial disparities in early life socioenvironmental conditions and verbal abilities.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
In this observational study, we will use data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS), a longitudinal, birth-cohort study from 20 large urban U.S. cities. For the current study, we will use data from 2,466 participants who have complete data on the loneliness measures at ages 5 and 9. Of these 2,466, 10 participants will drop out due to attending an ungraded high school. Therefore, our final sample will consist of 2,456 participants. 

We apply proportional odds logistic regression to address the first research question, and generalized propensity score weighting and g-computation to estimate the marginal effects of persistent and transient loneliness on educational achievement to explore the second question. 6888afd587ed957d07234146 Early-life adversity, childhood loneliness, and educational achievement.pdf https://osf.io/project/mqd2e/files/osfstorage/6888afd587ed957d07234146 https://osf.io/download/6888afd587ed957d07234146 86832e8d0bbc9bcff2105418c30eaac06ddb3f303892bd97de50272e45805b10

table.data_collection_procedures: We will use data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS), which is a longitudinal, birth-cohort study from 20 large urban U.S. cities. These cities were selected to represent all U.S. cities with a population of 200,000 or more. Data were collected at the hospital when the focal child was born, beginning in 1998. Additional data were collected, followed by telephone interviews and in-home assessments when the children reached ages 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, and 22. The original sample included 4,898 children. By design, FFCWS oversampled the children born to unmarried mothers (N = 3,711) compared to 1,187 children born to married parents.

table.measured_variables:
Childhood loneliness 

Loneliness was measured at years 5 and 9 with the item “Child complains of loneliness” from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL/4-18) (Achenbach, 1992). The item was answered by the child’s mother or principal caregiver, who was asked to indicate whether the statement was not true (=0), sometimes or somewhat true (=1), or very true or often true of her child (=2). Scores were dichotomized, considering values of 1 and 2 as reporting loneliness at that time point (=1), versus not reporting loneliness (=0). Based on scores from both waves, we created three childhood loneliness groups: “persistent loneliness” (n=168) if reporting loneliness at both time points, “transient loneliness” (n=603) if reporting loneliness at one time point, and “never lonely” during childhood (n=1,685). 

Predictors of childhood loneliness: Socio-environmental factors and verbal ability at year 5

Material hardship is a measure of to what extent basic needs are covered in the household, and the capability to meet expenses. It consists of eleven items answered by the child’s mother that explore if in the last 12 months there have been problems due to the unpayment of the rent or mortgage, unpayment of gas, oil or electricity bills, covering doctor visits or hospital stay expenses, if children or adults in the household had been on the need of receiving meals for free due to lack of money, or if there has been need to borrow money from friends or family to help pay bills. Answers were coded as 0=no, and 1=yes. Items will be summed, resulting in a score from 0 to 11 with higher scores indicating higher levels of material hardship.

Neighborhood collective efficacy (NCE) is a combined measure of social control (5 items - someone would intervene if: children were skipping school and hanging out on the street, children were spray-painting buildings, children were showing disrespect to an adult, a fight broke out in front of the house of building, the fire station closest to the neighborhood was threatened) and levels of cohesion and trust (4 items - neighbors are willing to help, it is a close-knit neighborhood, people generally get along with each other, people share the same values) in the neighborhood. Each item could be answered from 1=very likely to 4=very unlikely. We will sum the items to yield a total neighborhood collective efficacy score that could range from 9 to 38, with higher scores indicating lower neighborhood collective efficacy. Both mother and father completed the scale. In our study, we will use data reported by the mother, and in cases where data was missing, we used the father’s reported scores if these were available (a total of 195 mothers’ missing reports on this scale were filled with the father’s scores).

Child emotional and physical maltreatment was measured with three subscales from the Conflict Tactics Scale - Parent Child Version (CTS-PC) (Straus et al., 1998), informing about the frequency with which the primary caregiver used psychological aggression, physical assault, and neglect against the child in the past year. The primary caregiver was asked a series of questions about their behavior as well as the behavior of the other parent, for example “How often in the past year did you slap the child on the hand, arm, or leg?” with frequency response options ranging  from “it never happened” to “more than 20 times.” 

Each of the subscales consists of five items. In line with recommendations from the scale developer (Straus et al., 1998) we will assign the midpoint of the ranges in the following manner: responses of “never” and “not in the past year” will be coded as 0; “once” will be coded as 1; “twice” will be coded as 2; “3-5 times” will be coded as 4; “6-10 times” will be coded as 8; “11-20 times” will be coded as 15; and “20 or more times” will be coded as 25. The five questions for each subscale will then be added together to create an overall count of the number of times the form of abuse had occurred in the past year. 

Scores of material hardship, neighborhood collective efficacy, and child emotional and physical maltreatment will be standardized based on our study sample. 

Receptive vocabulary and verbal ability were measured with the third edition of the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT-III) (Dunn & Dunn, 1997). During the PPVT, the interviewer would read a word and ask the child to identify the picture that corresponds to that word among a set of four pictures on an easel or activity book. Child’s scores were computed based on the information recorded by the interviewer in Section B of the In-Home Activity Workbook (Bendheim-Thoman Center for Research and Wellbeing & Columbia Population Research Center, 2018). PPVT has been used as a measure of cognitive competence in early childhood and of school readiness (Razza et al., 2010). In our study, we will use PPVT raw scores and standardize them based on our study sample. 

Outcome of childhood loneliness: educational achievement 

Educational achievement will be assessed with three different outcomes reported by the young adult at the age of 22: out-of-school suspension, high school grades, and educational attainment.

Out-of-school suspension refers to whether the adolescent was temporarily excluded from school as a disciplinary action from 4th grade to 12th grade. That is after the age of 9, which is after the time of exposure in our study. This variable will be coded as 0 if the participant didn’t receive an out-of-school suspension or if this happened before 4th grade (n=34), and as 1 if the participant received an out-of-school suspension from 4th grade to 12th grade. 

High school grades are assessed with the question “What best represents your grades in high school?”. Originally, scores range from 1 (mostly D’s or lower) to 8 (mostly A’s). This variable will be dichotomized into half B’s/half Cs or lower (=1), and mostly B’s or higher (=0). 

Educational attainment is defined as the highest level of education completed by the age of 22, being 1=less than high school, 2=high school or equivalent, 3=some college or technical education, and 4=completed college or graduate school.


Confounders 

All models will include as confounders child’s sex (boy/girl), child’s race/ethnicity self-reported at age of 22 or age 15 if the age 22 self-report was missing (1=white non-Hispanic, 2=black/African American non-Hispanic, 3= Hispanic/Latino, 4=other non-Hispanic, 5=multi-racial non-Hispanic), mother’s age in years, mother’s ethnicity (1=white non-Hispanic, 2=black non-Hispanic, 3= Hispanic, 4=other), mother’s place of birth (outside the US: yes/no), parents’ relationship status (married, cohabiting not married, not cohabiting), and child’s low weight at birth (yes/no <2,500g). We will also include the following indicators measured at child’s age of 3: mother-reported child’s general health status (1=fair/poor health, 0=good/very good/excellent), and child’s physical disability (yes/no) (e.g., blindness, respiratory problems, speech problems, Down syndrome).

Moreover, we will include several measures regarding mother’s education, cognitive abilities and health state measured at child’s age of 3: educational attainment (1=less than HS, 2=HS or equivalent, 3=some college, tech;  4=college or graduate), cognitive ability (measured with the Similarities subtest of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale – Revised, WAIS-R), self-reported general health status (1=fair/poor health, 0=good/very good/excellent), and fulfilment of clinical criteria of major depressive episode (conservative criteria), generalized anxiety disorder, alcohol abuse, and drug abuse measured with the Composite International Diagnostic Interview - Short Form (CIDI-SF). The CIDI-SF is a standardized instrument for assessment of mental disorders intended for use in epidemiological, cross-cultural, and other research studies (Kessler et al., 1998). The CIDI questions for alcohol and drug dependence are based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 3rd Edition (DSM-III-R) (APA, 1987) diagnostic criteria, while the measures of major depressive episode and generalized anxiety disorder are based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) (APA, 1994). The final scores are a constructed binary variable in which respondents are classified as 1=probable cases, 0=probable non-cases.
table.statistical_tests:
To answer our first research question (Are early-life socio-environmental indicators and verbal abilities associated with childhood loneliness?), we will use data collected at birth, and at years 3, 5, and 9. We will fit several sets of ordinal proportional odds logistic regression models to explore if the socio-environmental indicators (material hardship, neighborhood collective efficacy, child’s emotional and physical maltreatment) and verbal ability scores at age 5 are associated with childhood loneliness at ages 5 and 9 (persistent, transient, or never) while adjusting for relevant confounders (measured at birth and year 3). For this, we will first fit three analogous models, including each one of the socio-environmental indicators as the predictor. Second, we will include the three socio-environmental indicators as predictors in the same regression model. Third, we will fit a model with verbal ability as the predictor. Fourth, we will run three analogous models, including one of three socio-environmental indicators, the verbal ability indicator, and an interaction term between each of the socio-environmental indicators and verbal ability. All models will include demographic variables and the mother’s and child’s characteristics at the child’s age of 3 as confounders. See Table 1 for a summary of all the planned regression models. The proportional odds assumption will be evaluated with the Brant-Wald test and by running stratified binomial regression models for “persistent or transient” versus “never” lonely, and “persistent” versus “transient or never” lonely to compare the differences in the predictor’s estimates between the two models. The analyses will be conducted across imputed datasets, and estimates will be pooled using Rubin’s rules. 

To answer the second research question (Are children who report persistent loneliness during childhood at a higher risk of later poorer educational achievement?), we will use data collected at birth and years 3, 5, 9, and 22. We will use propensity score weighting for covariate adjustment (step 1, design phase) before the estimation of the marginal effects of interest (step 2, analysis phase). As suggested in Nguyen & Stuart (2024), we will conduct multiple imputation as an early step (step 0) in our analysis. Then, we will estimate the propensity score weights in the imputed datasets for each of the exposure regimes (“within” method). 

Since we have a multilevel exposure, to achieve covariate balance among the three loneliness categories (persistent, transient, and never lonely), we will use Generalized Propensity Scores (GPSs) (Imbens, 2000; Imai & van Dyk, 2004). GPSs extend the traditional binary propensity score framework to multi-category exposures, allowing us to estimate the conditional probability of assignment to each childhood loneliness group given the observed covariates. These estimated probabilities can then be used to construct weights that generate a weighted pseudo-population in which the distribution of covariates is balanced across the loneliness categories.

Our generalized propensity score models will include as covariates: demographic variables, mother’s and child’s characteristics at the child’s age of 3, and socioenvironmental conditions and child’s verbal ability at the child’s age of 5. These variables are expected to be either related to educational attainment or both educational attainment and childhood loneliness (Bergstra et al., 2019; Brookhart et al., 2006). This decision is based on previous subject matter theory, so it will be independent of results arising from research question 1. Weight estimation will be conducted using different estimation methods whose performance will be compared in terms of achieved covariate balance (e.g., covariate balancing propensity scores, generalized boosted models). The objective will be to obtain absolute standardized mean differences of < 0.10 for all covariates in the weighted sample for each of the pairwise comparisons between exposure groups (i.e., persistent vs. never, persistent vs. transient, and transient vs never). We will consider stabilizing or truncating the weights in the case of extreme weights.

Finally, we will use weighted g-computation to estimate pairwise average treatment effects (ATE) (step 2) (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024; Greifer, 2025). The ATE of exposure a0 relative to exposure a1 refers to the comparison of mean outcomes had the entire population been observed under one exposure a0, versus had the entire population been observed under another exposure, a1 (McCaffrey et al., 2013). We will estimate three marginal ATEs per outcome (i.e., out-of-school suspension, high school average grades, and educational attainment at age 22), corresponding to the following pairwise contrasts: reporting persistent loneliness (a=2) during childhood compared to not reporting it (a=0), reporting persistent loneliness (a=2) compared to reporting transient loneliness (a=1), and reporting transient loneliness (a=1) compared to not reporting it (a=0). Estimation of confidence intervals will be done by bootstrapping. 

R packages mice (for multiple imputation), MatchThem (for estimation of the weights in the imputed datasets), weightIt (for propensity score and weight estimation), cobalt (for covariate balance assessment), and marginaleffects (for treatment effect estimation) will be used to conduct the analysis.
table.missing_data_handling:
We will use data from 2,466 participants who have complete data on the loneliness measures at ages 5 and 9. Of these 2,466, 10 participants will drop out due to attending an ungraded high school. Therefore, our final sample will consist of 2,456 participants. Remaining missing values in the final sample will be handled with multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE).

We will conduct multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) to handle remaining missing values in our final sample. The proportion of missing values varies across variables from less than 5% in covariates measured at birth and years 3 and 5, to up to 20% in the educational achievement variables measured at age 22. Given the overall proportion of missing values, we will estimate and conduct the analysis across 20 imputed datasets. The imputation model will include all the variables included in future analyses, plus NCE scores at year 3, Non-violent discipline subscale (CTS) scores at year 5, child’s PPVT scores at age of 9, and educational attainment reported by the primary caregiver at year 22 as auxiliary variables.

Based on scores from both waves, we created three childhood loneliness groups: “persistent loneliness” (n=168) if reporting loneliness at both time points, “transient loneliness” (n=603) if reporting loneliness at one time point, and “never lonely” during childhood (n=1,685).

Predictors of childhood loneliness: Socio-environmental factors and verbal ability at year 5

Material hardship is a measure of to what extent basic needs are covered in the household, and the capability to meet expenses. It consists of eleven items answered by the child’s mother that explore if in the last 12 months there have been problems due to the unpayment of the rent or mortgage, unpayment of gas, oil or electricity bills, covering doctor visits or hospital stay expenses, if children or adults in the household had been on the need of receiving meals for free due to lack of money, or if there has been need to borrow money from friends or family to help pay bills. Answers were coded as 0=no, and 1=yes. Items will be summed, resulting in a score from 0 to 11 with higher scores indicating higher levels of material hardship.

Neighborhood collective efficacy (NCE) is a combined measure of social control (5 items - someone would intervene if: children were skipping school and hanging out on the street, children were spray-painting buildings, children were showing disrespect to an adult, a fight broke out in front of the house of building, the fire station closest to the neighborhood was threatened) and levels of cohesion and trust (4 items - neighbors are willing to help, it is a close-knit neighborhood, people generally get along with each other, people share the same values) in the neighborhood. Each item could be answered from 1=very likely to 4=very unlikely. The primary caregiver was asked a series of questions about their behavior as well as the behavior of the other parent, for example “How often in the past year did you slap the child on the hand, arm, or leg?” with frequency response options ranging from “it never happened” to “more than 20 times.”

Each of the subscales consists of five items. In line with recommendations from the scale developer (Straus et al., 1998) we will assign the midpoint of the ranges in the following manner: responses of “never” and “not in the past year” will be coded as 0; “once” will be coded as 1; “twice” will be coded as 2; “3-5 times” will be coded as 4; “6-10 times” will be coded as 8; “11-20 times” will be coded as 15; and “20 or more times” will be coded as 25. text.text: We examine (1) whether indicators of early-life adversity are associated with children's loneliness complaints and their recurrence at ages 5 and 9; and (2) whether children's loneliness complaints are associated with poorer educational achievement measured at age 22 after adjusting for early-life adversity indicators.
We used data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (US, original sample n=4,898; study sample n=2,456).
Children's loneliness complaints were reported by the principal caregiver.
We applied (1) binomial logistic regression and (2) weighted g-computation.
In our sample, 6.8% of children had recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints.
Indicators of socioenvironmental early-life adversity were associated with higher odds of loneliness complaints.
Moreover, higher material hardship and lower neighborhood collective efficacy were associated with higher odds of complaints recurring at ages 5 and 9.
We observed no association between caregiverreported loneliness in childhood and later educational achievement.
We note limitations in our measurement of childhood loneliness.
Loneliness is a distressing experience that arises perceiving that one's interpersonal needs and expectations are not satisfied by one's interpersonal relationships (Cunningham et al., 2025).

text.text: Previous studies show that at age 5 children can provide valid definitions of loneliness, identify interpersonal contexts and associated aversive feelings (i.e., sadness, aloneness), as well as suggest ways of coping (i.e., make contact with others) (Cassidy & Asher, 1992; Qualter et al., 2015).

text.text: All three socioenvironmental factorsfamily material hardship, neighborhood quality, and child maltreatment -have been previously associated with poorer educational achievement (Brooks-Gunn & Duncan, 1997; Nieuwenhuis & Hooimeijer, 2016; Zhang et al., 2025).

text.text: Child's early-life cognitive ability is another potential confounder in the association between childhood loneliness and educational achievement.

Verbal ability is a strong predictor of school readiness and later educational success (Pace et al., 2017), and a previous prospective study observed that higher vocabulary in childhood predicted lower loneliness in adolescence (Fuhrmann et al., 2022).

text.text: Some evidence also suggests early-life language ability contribute to emotional and behavioral development in childhood (Clegg et al., 2015).

text.text: Notably, children from lower socioeconomic status families tend to show lower language skills than their peers by school entry (Pace et al., 2017).

text.text: Loneliness becomes problematic when it persists over time, contributing to further social withdrawal and disconnection (Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2010; Vanhalst et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Loneliness becomes problematic when it persists over time, contributing to further social withdrawal and disconnection <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Vanhalst et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Recurrent loneliness may even be more critical at a young age, given that loneliness shows a relatively high rank-order stability over the life span (Buecker et al., 2021; Mund et al., 2020), and that childhood and adolescence are sensitive periods for the development of social and cognitive skills and formation of social connections (Blakemore & Mills, 2014; Orben et al., 2020).

text.text: However, most of the previous studies exploring early-life adversity, loneliness, and educational achievement have been focused on adolescence and young adulthood.
Therefore, our study aims are twofold.

First, we explore whether three early-life socioenvironmental indicators and child's verbal ability are associated with child's caregiver-reported loneliness complaints, categorized as complaints recurring at both ages 5 and 9 (hereafter "recurrent"), transient (reported at only one of these ages), or not reported.

Second, we investigate whether caregiverreported loneliness complaints are associated with a higher risk of poorer educational achievement measured in young adulthood, adjusting for early-life socioenvironmental conditions and child's verbal ability as potential confounders.
We hypothesize that children whose caregivers report recurrent complaints of loneliness will more often come from poorer socioenvironmental contexts and have lower verbal ability.
Moreover, we expect these children to be at a higher risk of poorer educational achievement measured in young adulthood, even after considering initial disparities in early-life risk factors.

text.text: We leveraged data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS), a longitudinal birth-cohort study from 20 large urban U.S. cities.
These cities were selected to represent all U.S.
cities with a population of 200,000 or more.
Baseline data were collected at the hospital when the participating children were born, beginning in 1998.
Additional data were collected by telephone interviews and in-home assessments when the children reached ages 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, and 22.
The original sample included 4,898 children.
By design, FFCWS oversampled the children born to unmarried mothers (n = 3,710) compared to children born to married parents (n =1,187) (Reichman et al., 2001).
text.formatted: By design, FFCWS oversampled the children born to unmarried mothers (n = 3,710) compared to children born to married parents (n =1,187) <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Reichman et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Parents provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Follow-up and additional modules (e.g., home-visits) included additional consent forms.
For the current study, we used data from 2,466 children who had complete data on the loneliness measures at ages 5 and 9.
Of these 2,466, 10 participants were excluded due to attending an ungraded high school.
Therefore, our final sample consists of 2,456 participants.
Loneliness was measured at ages 5 and 9 with the item "Child complains of loneliness" from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL/4-18) (Achenbach, 1992).
text.formatted: Loneliness was measured at ages 5 and 9 with the item "Child complains of loneliness" from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL/4-18) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Achenbach, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: The item was answered by the child's mother or principal caregiver, who was asked to indicate whether the statement was not true (=0), sometimes or somewhat true (=1), or very true or often true of their child (=2).

Because only 5 caregivers reported the item as "very true or often true" at both time points, we dichotomized the scores, considering values of 1 and 2 as the caregiver reporting the child's loneliness complaints at that time point (=1), versus not reporting loneliness complaints (=0), to ensure enough participants in each exposure subgroup.

Based on scores from both waves, we created three groups: "recurrent" (n=168) if the caregiver reported loneliness complaints at both ages 5 and 9, "transient" (n=603) if the caregiver reported loneliness complaints at one time point, and "not reported" if the caregiver did not report loneliness complaints at either age (n=1,685).
Material hardship was a measure of to what extent basic needs are covered in the household and the capability to meet expenses.

It consisted of eleven items answered by the child's mother that explored if in the last 12 months there have been problems due to the unpayment of the rent or mortgage, unpayment of gas, oil or electricity bills, covering doctor visits or hospital stay expenses, if children or adults in the household had been on the need of receiving meals for free due to lack of money, or if there has been need to borrow money from friends or family to help pay bills.
Answers were coded as0=no, and1=yes.
We summed the items, resulting in a score from 0 to 11 with higher scores indicating higher levels of material hardship.

Neighborhood collective efficacy (NCE) was a combined measure of social control (5 itemssomeone would intervene if: children were skipping school and hanging out on the street, children were spray-painting buildings, children were showing disrespect to an adult, a fight broke out in front of the house of building, the fire station closest to the neighborhood was threatened) and levels of cohesion and trust in the neighborhood (4 items -neighbors are willing to help, it is a close-knit neighborhood, people generally do not get along with each other, people do not share the same values).
Each item could be answered from1=very likely to4=very unlikely.
Two items were reversed-coded.
We summed the items to yield a total neighborhood collective efficacy score that could range from 9 to 36, with higher scores indicating lower neighborhood collective efficacy.
Both mother and father completed the scale.

In our study, we used data reported by the mother, and in cases where data was missing, we used the father's reported scores if these were available (a total of 210 mothers' missing reports on this scale were filled with the father's scores).

Child emotional and physical maltreatment was measured with three subscales from the Conflict Tactics Scale -Parent Child Version (CTS-PC) (Straus et al., 1998) informing about the frequency with which the primary caregiver used psychological aggression, physical assault, and neglect against the child in the past year.

text.text: The primary caregiver was asked a series of questions about their behavior as well as the behavior of the other parent, for example, "How often in the past year did you slap the child on the hand, arm, or leg?"
with frequency response options ranging from "it never happened" to "more than 20 times".
Each of the subscales consisted of five items.

In line with recommendations from the scale developer (Straus et al., 1998) we assigned the midpoint of the ranges in the following manner: responses of "never" and "not in the past year" are coded as 0; "once" as 1; "twice" as 2; "3-5 times" as 4; "6-10 times" as 8; "11-20 times" as 15; and "20 or more times" as 25.

Final scores of material hardship, neighborhood collective efficacy, and child emotional and physical maltreatment were standardized (z-scores) within our study sample.
Receptive vocabulary and verbal ability were measured with the third edition of the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT-III) (Dunn & Dunn, 1997).

text.text: During the PPVT, the interviewer would read a word and ask the child to identify the picture that corresponds to that word among a set of four pictures on an easel or activity book.

Child's scores were computed based on the information recorded by the interviewer in Section B of the In-Home Activity Workbook (Bendheim-Thoman Center for Research and Wellbeing & Columbia Population Research Center, 2018).

text.text: In our study, we used the PPVT raw scores and standardized (z-scores) them within our study sample.

Out-of-school suspension referred to whether the participant was temporarily excluded from school as a disciplinary action between the 4 th and the 12 th grade, that is, after the time of exposure in our study (i.e., after age 9).

This variable was coded as 0 if the participant didn't receive an out-of-school suspension or if this happened before 4 th grade (n=34), and as 1 if the participant received an out-ofschool suspension between the 4 th and the 12 th grade.
High school grades were assessed with the question "What best represents your grades in high school?".
Originally, the scores ranged from 1 (mostly D's or lower) to 8 (mostly A's).
This variable was dichotomized into half B's/half Cs or lower (=1), and mostly B's or higher (=0).

Educational attainment was defined as the highest level of education completed by the age of 22, being1=less than high school,2=high school or equivalent,3=some college or technical education, and4=completed college or graduate school.
We dichotomized the scores into high school/equivalent or lower (=1), and some college/technical education or higher (=0).

text.text: First, we handled missing values in our final sample using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), including all study variables and four auxiliary variables (i.e., NCE at age 3, non-violent discipline CTS's subscale at age 5, child's PPVT at age 9, and educational attainment reported by the primary caregiver at age 22), obtaining 20 imputed datasets.

To answer our first research question we used data collected at birth, and at ages 3, 5, and 9 to fit several sets of binomial logistic regression models to explore associations of early-life adversity indicators with the likelihood of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints ("recurrent or transient"
versus "not reported") and with the likelihood of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints recurring at ages 5 and 9 ("recurrent" versus "transient or not reported").

For each comparison, we first ran three analogous models, including one of the socioenvironmental indicators (i.e., material hardship, neighborhood collective efficacy, and child maltreatment) as the predictor (Models 1-3).
Second, we included the three socioenvironmental indicators as predictors in the same regression model (Model 4).
Third, we fit a model with verbal ability as the predictor (Model 5).

Fourth, we ran three analogous models, including one of three socioenvironmental indicators, the verbal ability indicator, and an interaction term between each of the socioenvironmental indicators and verbal ability (Models 6-8).
We had no prior hypotheses on the direction or magnitude of the interaction.
All models were adjusted for all the demographic variables and the mother's and child's characteristics at the child's age of 3.

To examine associations between caregiver-reported loneliness complaints and educational achievement measured in young adulthood (research question 2), we used data collected at birth and at ages 3, 5, 9, and 22.
There are several potential sources of confounding, and we aimed to adjust for all measured confounders.

To achieve covariate balance among the three loneliness complaints groups, we used Generalized Propensity Scores (GPSs) (Imbens, 2000; Imai & van Dyk, 2004), which extend the traditional binary propensity score framework to multi-category exposures, allowing us to estimate the probability of assignment to each group given the observed covariates.

text.text: Propensity scores are a method for covariate adjustment that is particularly useful when adjusting for a high number of covariates, as they summarize the high-dimensional covariate information into a single score representing the probability of the exposure given the observed covariates.
In our case, the propensity scores are used to weight individuals according to the probability of receiving the exposure given the observed covariates.
This weighting creates a pseudo-population in which the distribution of confounders is independent of the exposure, aiming to resemble the balance expected under a randomized experiment.

An important advantage of propensity score weighting is that covariate balance can be directly assessed after weighting, typically by plotting the standardized mean differences across exposure groups.
This allows comparison of alternative model specifications and the selection of the specification that achieves the best balance with the data at hand.
In addition, modern implementations allow the use of flexible, data-adaptive methods (e.g., machine learning algorithms) to estimate the propensity score.

These methods can capture nonlinearities and interactions without requiring the analyst to prespecify them, increasing the likelihood of correct model specification and improving confounding control (Greifer, 2025).

First, minimally adjusted, including child's sex, child's race/ethnicity, mother's age, and parental relationship status at birth.

Second, fully adjusted, including an array of covariates expected to be either related to young adulthood educational achievement or both educational achievement and childhood loneliness based on previous subject matter theory (Bergstra et al., 2019).

text.text: The ATE of exposure a0 relative to exposure a1 refers to the comparison of mean outcomes had the entire population been observed under one exposure, a0, versus had the entire population been observed under another exposure, a1 (McCaffrey et al., 2013).

text.text: G-computation is commonly used in settings with time-varying exposure and time-varying confounders affected by prior exposure, where standard stratification-based regression adjustment yields biased estimates.

In a simpler setting like ours, where all variables are measured at baseline, gcomputation is still useful because it targets the marginal exposure-outcome association (populationaverage) rather than the conditional association (covariate-specific).

We focus on marginal associations because they correspond to contrasts between the expected potential outcomes under exposure a1 and a0 in the entire population, whereas conditional associations describe the association within covariate strata, that is, within individuals with a fixed set of covariate values (Greifer, 2025).

text.text: Conditional effects can be harder to interpret, especially when the model includes non-linear terms or interactions.

Furthermore, the g-computation framework can be combined with flexible or nonparametric estimators (e.g., machine-learning methods) for the outcome or propensity score models, which reduces reliance on strict parametric assumptions and increases the likelihood of correct model specification (Snowden et al., 2011).

text.text: Early-life socioenvironmental factors and child's verbal ability as predictors of caregiverreported loneliness complaints (recurrent, transient, or not reported at ages 5 and 9) (RQ1) All three early-life socioenvironmental indicators at age 5 were associated with higher odds of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints in middle childhood.

The odds of loneliness complaints (either recurrent or transient at ages 5 and 9) were 19% greater per 1 SD increase in child maltreatment scores (OR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.09-1.30), 17% greater per 1 SD increase in material hardship (OR: 1.17, 95% CI: 1.07-1.28) and 16% greater per 1 SD decrease in neighborhood collective efficacy (OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.06-1.27).

Additionally, material hardship (OR: 1.39, 95% CI: 1.21-1.60) and lower neighborhood collective efficacy (OR: 1.20, 95% CI: 1.02-1.40) were associated with higher odds of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints recurring at ages of 5 and 9.

In the case of child maltreatment, the odds of recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints compared to transient/no reported loneliness were 16% greater (OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 0.99-1.36), but the confidence interval included the null value.
The magnitude of these estimates remained similar when including all socioenvironmental predictors in the same model.

text.text: In our study, we used data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study spanning 22 years since birth to answer two connected research questions.
We first observed that material hardship, low neighborhood collective efficacy, and child maltreatment were associated with higher odds of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints.
Moreover, material hardship and low neighborhood collective efficacy were also associated with the recurrence of these complaints at ages 5 and 9.
However, we did not observe an association between caregiver-reported loneliness complaints and educational achievement measured in young adulthood.
This may be partly due to limitations in how loneliness was measured, particularly its reliance on a single caregiver-reported item.

Our results are in line with previous studies highlighting the relevance of early-life environment for youth's social connection and well-being (Donnelly et al., 2016; Hjalmarsson & Mood, 2015; Schneider et al., 2017).

text.text: In our study, material hardship, neighborhood conditions, and child maltreatment appeared as independent predictors of later caregiver-reported loneliness complaints.
Moreover, we observed that material hardship and low neighborhood collective efficacy were associated with higher odds of recurrent loneliness complaints at ages 5 and 9.
In sex-stratified analysis, we observed that these associations had larger effect sizes among girls.

While child's verbal ability was not associated with caregiver-reported loneliness complaints, it moderated the association of material hardship with loneliness complaints: the association was greater among children with higher levels of verbal ability.
Due to the exploratory nature of these models, results should be interpreted with caution.
A plausible post hoc explanation is that children with higher verbal ability are more capable of engaging in complex relational comparisons and communicating their experiences of loneliness.
In sex-stratified analysis, the moderating role of child's verbal ability was observed among boys only.

Regarding our second research question, we did not find evidence of an association between caregiver-reported loneliness complaints and educational achievement measured in young adulthood, in contrast to the associations previously reported in adolescent samples (Eccles et al., 2023; Frostad et al., 2015; Jefferson et al., 2023; Jefferson et al., 2023; Matthews et al., 2023).

text.text: This was not merely a result of a strict covariate adjustment since there was no evidence for an association in the minimally adjusted outcome models either.
Our study differs from previous ones in other aspects that might have been key.
First, while our exposure was measured at ages 5 and 9, previous studies explored loneliness later in life, from age 11 onwards, and mostly during adolescence.
Children tend to conceptualize loneliness in terms that are closer to objective social isolation (Cassidy & Asher, 1992; Verity et al., 2021).

text.text: The association with educational achievement may only emerge later in life, when loneliness becomes more prevalent, peer acceptance gains more relevance, sensitivity for social threats increases, and the educational context becomes more demanding (Qualter et al., 2015 (Qualter et al., , 2025)).

text.text: Second, we used self-reported indicators of educational achievement measured in young adulthood while several previous studies used indicators of aptitude and well-being at school measured at a younger age.

For instance, Eccles et al. (2023) reported an association of higher levels of loneliness with poorer self-reported achievement perception, higher feelings of school dissatisfaction, and greater feelings of school pressure, and Frostad et al. (2015) explored the association of loneliness with the intention to leave school at age 16.

text.text: Recurrent loneliness may make the individual more prone to cognitive biases, lower self-esteem, and hypersensitivity to social threats (Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2010).
text.formatted: Recurrent loneliness may make the individual more prone to cognitive biases, lower self-esteem, and hypersensitivity to social threats <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, loneliness could have stronger associations with measures that refer to educational perceptions, motivations, and attitudes than with measures that refer to the actual educational performance.

Nevertheless, negative perceptions of one's educational capabilities may represent a risk factor for poorer academic trajectories, through pathways such as reduced classroom engagement due to perceived exclusion, avoidance of collaborative learning, and heightened stress responses in peer-evaluative settings.

Third, several previous studies have used measures that assess school loneliness specifically (Frostad et al., 2015; Jefferson et al., 2023), while in our study child's complaints of loneliness were reported by their mothers.

text.text: Future studies could benefit from exploring associations with different dimensions of loneliness and types of interpersonal relationships (i.e., school, family, or peer-related loneliness) (Cunningham et al., 2025).

text.text: Finally, all previous studies used European samples (i.e., UK, Denmark, Norway) compared to ours from the United States, and cultural differences might also underlie the different results.
This pre-registered study leverages data from an ethnically diverse sample of children born in the US, followed since birth to young adulthood.
The availability of several health and social measures permitted us to adjust our analysis for several known confounders of our associations of interest.
The sensitivity analyses showed the robustness of the conclusions drawn from our main analysis.
Our study has several limitations.
First, although single-item loneliness measures are considered reliable (Mund et al., 2023), the only measure of childhood loneliness available in the FFCWS was reported by the child's mother.
text.formatted: First, although single-item loneliness measures are considered reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mund et al., 2023)</ref>, the only measure of childhood loneliness available in the FFCWS was reported by the child's mother.

text.text: This may have introduced reporting bias, as caregiver-reported loneliness complaints may not fully reflect the subjective experience of loneliness felt by the children themselves.

In addition, although single-item loneliness measures are considered reliable (Mund et al., 2023), loneliness comprises social, emotional, and cognitive aspects (Cunningham et al., 2025) and our operationalization obscured potential associations with later educational outcomes driven by any one specific facet.

text.text: Additionally, caregivers are not independent observers of the family relational context, and relying on mother's self-report might have introduced social desirability bias.
Also, it is possible that our loneliness measure mainly captured family-related loneliness, which might not necessarily translate into other social contexts.
Previous studies suggest that relationship problems carry over to other contexts, and have observed associations between parent-and peer-related loneliness in adolescents (Geukens et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous studies suggest that relationship problems carry over to other contexts, and have observed associations between parent-and peer-related loneliness in adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Geukens et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, other studies have found peer-and familyrelated loneliness to be associated with different outcomes (e.g., different psychopathology symptoms in Lasgaard et al., (2011)).
text.formatted: However, other studies have found peer-and familyrelated loneliness to be associated with different outcomes (e.g., different psychopathology symptoms in <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lasgaard et al., (2011)</ref>).

text.text: Similarly, peer-related and family-related loneliness might have different implications for later educational attainment, and in that case, our study may have failed to capture such implications.
Second, our categorization of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints as recurrent, transient, or not reported was based on just two measurement points, four years apart (at ages 5 and 9).

This may not adequately capture the real-life developmental trajectories of loneliness during these years, as recurrence at ages 5 and 9 does not imply persistence but may instead reflect intermittent distress.
Furthermore, to delimit our exposure groups, we classified children as "lonely" at each time point if their caregiver reported complaints of loneliness "sometimes" or "often".
Although this dichotomization made our statistical approach feasible, we lost information on the intensity or frequency of the reported complaints.
Altogether these compromise construct validity and the interpretation of group comparisons.
Third, despite the efforts to adjust for all potential sources of confounding, we cannot completely rule out the possibility of unmeasured or residual confounding biasing our results.
Thus, our results should be interpreted without making causal attributions.
This is common in observational studies due to the absence of randomization.
For instance, father's health status, educational attainment, or cognitive abilities could be potential unmeasured confounders of the associations examined in this study.

Fourth, the long interval of 11 years between caregiver-reported loneliness complaints and educational achievement measures may have failed to capture shorter-term consequences of loneliness that are not long-lasting and may have increased the risk of unmeasured confounding.
Fifth, the generalized propensity scores in the sex-stratified analysis did not reach good covariate balance due to few boys in the recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness group.

Sixth, we have estimated standard errors treating weights as fixed (i.e., ignoring uncertainty in their estimation) (Greifer, 2025) as the combination of bootstrapping and generalized boosted models was not computationally feasible.
text.formatted: Sixth, we have estimated standard errors treating weights as fixed (i.e., ignoring uncertainty in their estimation) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Greifer, 2025)</ref> as the combination of bootstrapping and generalized boosted models was not computationally feasible.

text.text: Seventh, these results from a solely US-based sample might not be generalizable to other populations.

Additionally, although our findings from the complete case analysis were similar to those obtained after multiple imputation, there is a risk of selection bias in our analytic sample that multiple imputation cannot resolve.
The attrition analysis suggested systematic differences between the original FFCWS sample and selected study participants.

It is plausible that children experiencing more severe adversities or recurrent loneliness complaints were also the most difficult to retain, which may have resulted in an attenuation of the associations observed in our sample.
Growing up in a family facing material hardships or experiencing child maltreatment in early life was associated with a higher risk of caregiver-reported loneliness complaints at ages 5 and 9.
Moreover, material hardship was associated with recurrent caregiver-reported loneliness complaints at both time points.
This is in line with previous studies emphasizing the relevance of early-life conditions for loneliness.
However, caregiver-reported loneliness complaints did not independently predict educational achievement measured in young adulthood.

Future studies in other populations that use child-reported assessments of loneliness, incorporate a multidimensional operationalization of loneliness, include measures of loneliness spanning from childhood to adolescence, and combine different indicators of educational success and school wellbeing (e.g., perceptions, motivations, school performance) are needed to further clarify these associations.
